conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be helping you through this admission for your 17th cycle of methotrexate. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’m okay—just a bit tired. The foot pain’s still there, but I’m used to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see you’ve had that burning pain in your right foot and leg for a while. We’ll keep managing that with gabapentin and oxycodone as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it helps, but it doesn’t go away completely. Is there any new test we’re doing this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a brain MRI before admission to check your lymphoma. Good news—it’s stable, no new lesions. So we’re on track with treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried it might be getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring closely. Today, you’ll get your methotrexate infusion—8 grams per square meter. We’ll give anti-nausea meds first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I usually get a little nauseous, but the ondansetron helps. Will I need to stay long after the infusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll stay for observation. We start IV fluids and sodium bicarbonate to help clear the methotrexate faster and protect your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the leucovorin? When does that start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: 24 hours after the chemo starts. It helps protect your healthy cells. We’ll check your methotrexate levels daily until they drop below 0.2.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my aspirin? I remember last time we stopped it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re holding your aspirin during the hospital stay to help the methotrexate clear better. You’ll restart it tomorrow after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. And my ulcerative colitis—should I restart the mesalamine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. After your flare last cycle, we switched to rectal mesalamine, which helped stop the bleeding. You’ve been off it since, and no symptoms now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried about another flare during chemo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The infusion went smoothly. You’re doing well. We’ll keep the IV fluids going and monitor your labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. Any side effects I should watch for tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching for nausea, mouth sores, or low blood counts. But your levels so far look stable. Liver enzymes are slightly up, but that’s expected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your first methotrexate level came back at 2.1—right on track. We’ve started leucovorin as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that a safe level? I know we want it to go down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfectly normal at this stage. It should drop quickly with the fluids and bicarbonate. We’ll check again tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my kidney function? I know methotrexate can affect that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is normal—0.7—and your urine output is good. No signs of kidney stress. Your clearance rate was actually high this cycle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I’ve been drinking extra fluids like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Staying hydrated really helps. We also gave you potassium—your level was a bit low yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your latest methotrexate level is 0.21—almost below the target. One more dose of leucovorin, and we’ll recheck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So close! Does that mean I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, once the level is under 0.2, you’re safe to leave. The next draw is in an hour. Fingers crossed!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—your methotrexate level is now <0.1. You don’t need any more leucovorin or bicarbonate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful! So I’m ready to go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Almost. We’ll finalize your discharge paperwork. Remember to restart your aspirin tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And stop it two days before the next chemo, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s to help the methotrexate clear faster. We’ll also continue heparin shots while you’re in the hospital for DVT prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember—because of my history with blood clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Your labs today look stable—mild anemia, but no change from before. Liver enzymes are up a bit, but that’s typical with chemo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my depression? I’ve been taking citalopram regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You seem emotionally stable, and you’re continuing the citalopram. That’s important—mental health is part of your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re cleared to go home. Keep taking your regular meds except aspirin—start that tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Rest up, and we’ll see you for your next cycle. Call if you have fever, severe pain, or anything concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll keep managing the foot pain with gabapentin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and use the oxycodone if needed. We’ll reassess if the pain worsens. Take care!

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again. See you next month.
